The opinion is centrally about no-knock/knock-and-announce doctrine: it states that the Court must decide whether the Fourth Amendment imposes a higher standard when a no-knock entry destroys property.
The opinion expressly builds from Wilson and Richards and applies Richards' reasonable-suspicion standard, so the Knock-and-Announce home with a Progeny role is supported.
The opinion says: "We hold that it does not" after framing the question as whether a no-knock entry involving property destruction requires a higher Fourth Amendment standard.
The opinion further states that Richards reasonable suspicion "depends in no way on whether police must destroy property in order to enter."
The separate caveat is supported by the opinion's statement that "Excessive or unnecessary destruction of property in the course of a search may violate the Fourth Amendment".
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Could add that suppression of fruits is not automatic for excessive destruction, matching the opinion's caveat.
